translations.text: A eulogy delivered by the honored patriarch and chief teacher, Apa Celestine, archbishop of the city of Rome.
He delivered it in praise of the martyrs’ glory and Christ’s true crown-bearer, the holy virgin, Saint Victor the general.
He delivered it on the day of his holy commemoration, which is the twenty-seventh day of the month of Pharmouthi.
He delivered it in his martyr shrine, which the God-loving emperor built for him in Rome.
He also spoke again about the consolation of the soul, making it clear that nothing in human life is lasting except suffering and hardship.
He also spoke about what is written in the Apostle: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of God,”
and about the great helplessness of a person at the moment when he gives his spirit into the hands of God.
He delivered this eulogy while Emperor Valentinian was seated beside him, together with the entire senate and all the people, men and women.
They were celebrating the festival of the general, [?] Saint Victor. Indeed, they were marveling at the wisdom of Saint Celestine. In the peace of God.
May his holy blessings come down upon us, and may we all be saved together. Amen. Bless us.
Whenever the Maker himself, the savior of his creation, the patient one who is full of every kind of compassion,
chooses in his compassion to remember the work of his hands and give them their food at the proper time,
and opens his hand, which is full of every kind of righteousness, and causes the sky to pour down rainwater at the proper time,
in this way the fields become green and blossom, and all humanity rejoices.
The loosening of the earth with rainwater in its season.
The farmer breaks up the clods of the field with the plow, and they cast seed into it at sowing time. It begins to bring forth sown seeds, each according to its kind.
And great delight comes to everyone,
so that they enjoy their food and their bodily sustenance—even the animals of the fields—
they leap and bound as they eat the grass of the sowing season.
And the farmers rejoice greatly, confident that they can pay their taxes from their fields.
If such joy comes from bodily food, then how great is today's joy, O flock of rational sheep,
and blessed people of the Christians, because the blood that came from God's side, together with the water, fell upon the earth!
It made the world new again and became a spring of water gushing forth into eternal life.
All humanity rejoiced, and they all leaped for joy.
They blossomed again through the water and the blood that came out of Emmanuel’s side.
They brought forth spiritual fruits, which are the virtues of the Holy Spirit.
Some chose purity for themselves from their birth to the end of their lives.
Others have wives but live like those who have none.
Some practice ascetic discipline from their youth to their old age through rigorous fasting.
Some renounced the world.
They went to the mountains.
They became monks, training themselves in the good struggle until the day of their death.
Others took up their crosses and followed the Lord.
They poured out their blood for their confession of God and received the crown of martyrdom.
In short, all humanity blossomed and bore fruit with great joy.
The written word was fulfilled in this generation: “They will all know [?], from the least to the greatest.”
For our Savior is among us today with his angels, celebrating the military commander Apa Victor on the day of his commemoration, which is today.
All the heavenly ranks are gathered with us today.
They honor the one who renounced the world and his possessions and received the perfect kingdom.
The prophets and martyrs are among us today, celebrating the one who renounced the world and its riches.
Christ loved him and crowned him with the crown of the kingdom of heaven.
O military commander, Saint Victor!
O crowned one among the martyrs!
O unrivaled master of the contest!
O true crown-bearer of Christ!
O one who made his body a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God!
I want to speak praises of you at your festival today, but I am afraid that I cannot cross the ocean of your achievements.
Since my tongue is a tongue of flesh, and the heart within me is a human heart, I cannot describe your glory and the honor with which God has clothed you.
Who among all the wise people of the world could ever describe your honor fully, O Saint Victor?
For you have been a virgin since your childhood.
You are a remarkable ascetic.
You fasted for two days at a time throughout your life.
The door of your house was open to everyone.
For this reason I am afraid to launch my boat onto the sea of your virtues.
I know the weakness of my tongue and of my heart, which has no wisdom in it.
In what way shall I honor you and praise you?
You are a virgin like Elijah, and you have never joined yourself to a woman.
You are righteous and good, and considerate toward all the poor, like Abraham the patriarch.
You are a mighty martyr among all the martyrs.
You were not afraid of kings, military commanders, or governors, nor could the tortures change your resolve.
The threats of your father Romanus could not turn you against your true father, Christ. Instead, you remained firmly grounded on the unshakable rock, Christ, until your last breath.
O righteous man in his generation, who made his body a sacrifice to God!
What shall I say, or what shall I declare about you, O Saint Victor?
If I compare you to Noah, you became perfect like him in your generation.
If I compare you to Abraham, you are hospitable like him, for God visited Abraham with his angels because of his hospitality.
You too, O Saint Victor: Christ, the Son of God, came to you in the appearance of a poor man.
He comforted you in the fortress in a desert land because of the great sufferings you endured for his holy name.
If I compare you to Isaac the patriarch, his father took him against his will to offer him up as a sacrifice to the Lord.
But you, O Saint Victor, of your own free choice,
offered up your body as a burnt offering to the Lord through the many tortures you endured for the name of Christ.
If I compare you to Jacob the patriarch, Christ took his name from him.
But in you, O Saint Victor, all the martyrs in heaven took pride, as did those on earth, because of your endurance.
If I compare you to Joseph, you fought against the passions as he did.
Joseph was handed over into slavery by his brothers.
But you, O Saint Victor, were handed over by your father because of the name of Christ.
Joseph attained kingship because of his endurance.
But you, O Saint Victor, attained the kingdom of heaven.
If I compare you to Melchizedek and Aaron, they offered up sheep and calves as symbols.
But you, O Saint Victor, made your own body an offering to God.
Because of this, you received great glory in the kingdom of heaven.
If I compare you to Moses the lawgiver, you too renounced military command in this world, your parents’ wealth, and your possessions.
You took up your cross and followed your Lord.
Moses did not want to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. Instead, he chose to suffer with the people of God rather than enjoy sin for a time.
You too, O Saint Victor, did not want to be called the son of Romanus, who was first in greeting the king.
You renounced the dignity of military command and your wealth.
You followed the one who said, “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.”
You received the rank of commander that lasts forever.
If I compare you to Isaiah the prophet, you too saw the one seated above the cherubim and seraphim.
He came to you and saved you from all your afflictions.
And he gave you glory in heaven and on earth.
In heaven, he made you commander among all the martyrs, as we will explain to you as the discourse proceeds.
He also glorified you on earth, so that your fragrance fills all the regions of the world,
and shrines are built for you everywhere, and great miracles and wonders take place through them.
To the glory of God and his holy martyr.
For the written saying is true: “Whoever gives me glory, my Father will honor him.”
Since you spent your whole life without involving yourself in the cares of this world, but devoted all your zeal to the love of God,
God therefore bestowed this great gift on you: he placed in your sanctuary a power that heals souls and bodies.
For you heal bodily illnesses through the grace that God has given you, and the illnesses of the soul as well, which are sins,
you cleanse through the signs and wonders that you reveal in your shrine in the four corners of the world.
O Saint Victor, your blood that was poured out toppled the pillar of Baal, as Elijah did, and you destroyed the idols and the pillars.
You became a pillar of the entire company of martyrs.
You extinguished the flame of the fire through the power of God who is with you, like the three saints.
To whom in Scripture, then, shall I compare you and find that you are not his equal? For I will not say that you surpass him.
What shall I say about you, O healer of hidden and visible illnesses?
Indeed, he even raised the dead with the oil of the lamp in his shrine, where you are gathered today. And I saw the wonder with my own eyes.
I am the least of all.
But let no one disbelieve the wonder that happened, lest the written saying be fulfilled concerning him: “The unbeliever does not have even a single obol.”
Listen now, and I will explain the matter to you, to the glory of God and Saint Victor, whose feast we celebrate today.
For indeed our Savior said, “Whoever believes in [?], the works I do in my Father’s name,
he too will do them, and he will do greater works than these.”
There was a man in this city whose name was Alexander.
He was exceedingly rich in gold and silver.
Now this man had a wife who was barren.
She had never borne a child, and they were deeply grieved about this because they had no heir to their property.
They heard about the mighty deeds and miracles taking place at the shrine of Saint Apa Victor.
They got up together and went to the holy place.
They brought their offerings into the shrine on Sunday.
Afterward they made a vow, saying, “Listen to us today as we plead with you.
If your mercy reaches us and you give us offspring, we will dedicate him to your shrine until the day of his death.
Only take away our disgrace and grant us our request.”
After saying these things, they went home joyfully.
Then one day Saint Victor interceded with Christ on their behalf.
The woman gave birth to a son who was very beautiful to look at, and the grace of God surrounded him.
They named him Victor, after Saint Victor.
There was great joy in their house, and they distributed abundant alms to the poor.
When the little boy reached [?] years of age, his parents could not bring themselves to give the little boy to the sanctuary of Saint Apa Victor,
as they had said they would. Instead, they went back on their vow.
They did not remember what is written: “Take care to fulfill what comes out of your mouth, for the Lord will closely examine your ways and punish you.”
Then the little boy's father and mother spoke to one another, saying,
“Look, we could not bring ourselves to give the little boy to the sanctuary as we had vowed.”
Let us summon someone in the city who buys slaves. Let him put a price on the little boy, and let us give his value to the holy place so that the martyr will not be angry with us.”
So they got up and summoned a merchant in the city who bought slaves and had sold them all his life.
He valued the little boy at forty gold coins, and they took the gold
and gave it to the martyr’s holy place.
They did not remember what is written: “If you make a vow to the Lord your God, you must fulfill it.”
When Saint Victor saw that the little boy’s parents had not fulfilled their vow honestly,
but thought that God’s gift could be acquired with money,
he caused the following thing to happen as a punishment for their foolishness.
One day the little boy was in the street, playing with children his own age near his parents’ house.
Suddenly a large stone from the [?] in the house fell on the little boy.
He fell and died immediately.
When his parents heard, they tore their clothes and cried out loudly.
They came out with the servants.
They found the little boy dead.
Oh, how great was the grief at that moment!
They cried out, “Woe to us, beloved son!
We are responsible for your death, because we made a vow and did not fulfill our vow to dedicate you to the holy one’s shrine.
Look, he has taken you away from us before we had our fill of you.
He has burned our hearts with grief for our beloved son.
We are the ones who deserve to die.
We do not know what we will do from this moment on.”
But his father took hold of a firm faith.
He took his little son into his arms, while the boy’s mother and his servants followed him.
They brought him into the shrine of Saint Victor.
He laid him down before the altar.
He cried out, saying, “Saint Victor, I know that you have power to do everything, and you are the one who granted me this little boy.
Do not deal with me according to my foolishness, but have compassion on my tears and return the little boy’s soul to him once again.
And we, together with him, will serve you until the day of our death.”
After saying these things while weeping, he took a little oil from the lamp.
He marked the little boy with it and put it on his mouth, his nose, and his heart.
The miracle that happened at that moment surpassed those of Elijah and Elisha.
For as soon as the oil from the lamp touched the little boy, the one who said, “I wound, and my hand heals,” [?].
Restore the little boy’s soul once more. And through the prayers of Saint Victor, he opened his eyes.
Great was the joy that came upon his parents that day, and upon everyone belonging to their household.
They cried out loudly, “You are great, O God of Saint Victor, and there is no other besides you in heaven or on earth!”
In place of sorrow, you have given us joy.
You raised the little boy for his parents after he had died.
When the crowd saw the great miracle that had happened, they cried out in a loud voice.
They ran toward the little boy.
They cried out, saying, “The God of Saint Victor is one!”
The little boy’s father went around the whole city with him, holding his hand and proclaiming the miracles of Saint Victor.
Afterward, he went to his house.
He brought all his possessions and his slaves.
He brought them into the sanctuary of Saint Victor.
He continued serving him until the day of his death. The little boy became an exemplary man and remained a virgin all his life.
Afterward, he attained the rank of priest. It was said about him that he had seen Saint Victor many times, appearing to him.
For the words our Savior spoke are indeed true: “My Father will honor whoever serves me.”
You see, my beloved, how powerful the intercession of Saint Victor is.
God punishes anyone who makes a vow and does not fulfill it.
We too, if we make a vow to the martyrs,
must fulfill it diligently, so that they do not become angry with us.
For it is a great sin to make a vow and then go back on what you have vowed.
But so that we do not linger over this subject,
let us return and tell you another great miracle that happened in the shrine of Saint Victor, to the glory of God and his holy martyrs.
There was a woman in this city named Callieutropia. She was the daughter of the sister of Emperor Honorius.
She was extremely wealthy.
One day, she happened to be sleeping at noon in her house, in an underground chamber, during the summer.
A demon sprang into both her breasts.
They swelled and became extremely bloated.
They hardened and became as hard as stone, hanging from her.
She kept weeping in great torment day and night.
She paid out large sums to the doctors.
No treatment helped her; instead, she remained in torment.
Her family gave up on her.
The physicians, in particular, made every effort, but they could not heal her, even though she was the king’s sister.
But they were powerless against the suffering caused by the illness, as it is written about them: “Their wisdom failed them.”
When she heard about the miracles and wonders taking place in the sanctuary of Saint Victor, she begged her husband and her brother
to let her go to the saint's sanctuary, so that perhaps his mercy would reach her and he would grant her healing.
Her family agreed to her request.
They saw that she was in danger of dying.
They ordered that she be placed in a litter and taken to the shrine of Saint Victor.
When she entered the shrine, she cried out, “My lord, Saint Victor, I beg you, have mercy on me and remove this suffering from me, for you are a saint of God.”
In the middle of the night, Saint Victor took pity on the woman’s misfortune.
He brought her rest.
She fell asleep, with her servants and eunuchs around her.
He came to her in a vision, wearing a purple robe and radiating rays of light, with a staff of light in his hand.
He said to her, “If you want to get well,
when you rise early tomorrow, take a little oil from the lamp burning before the altar and anoint your breasts.
The demon will be disturbed and come out, and you will be free of this suffering.
But take care [?] not to be hard-hearted toward your servants. And take care not to walk with your neck held high again, and stretch out your hand to the poor.
For this suffering came upon you because of your lack of mercy and your pride.”
The woman became greatly troubled.
She answered fearfully, “Who are you, appearing like this, with such great glory surrounding you?”
He answered in a gentle voice, “I am Victor, the commander of the great King.”
And when he said these things, she stopped looking at him.
Immediately she awoke from the vision.
She smelled a strong, sweet fragrance that had filled the entire martyr’s shrine, and she said to herself, “Truly, it was Saint Victor who was speaking with me,
a sinner.”
Immediately she woke her family.
She told them about the vision.
When morning came, she went to the [?] priest of the martyr’s shrine.
He gave her a little oil from the lamp.
When he placed it in her hands, she anointed her breasts, saying, “In the name of the God of Saint Victor, whose glory I was worthy to see, grant me healing.”
Immediately the demon became agitated.
It sprang out of her breasts like a vulture, while the people watched it looking like a flame of fire. Immediately her breasts returned to their normal condition.
She cried out, saying, “The God of Saint Victor is one!”
She also gave precious gifts to the martyr’s shrine: a great deal of gold and silver, to commemorate the healing she had received.
Afterward she went home to her family, glorifying God and his holy martyr.
It is also necessary for us to tell you about another great miracle that took place through this holy man.
When Emperor Honorius saw the healing his sister had received through Saint Victor, he rejoiced greatly.
And she pleased him by reinforcing the apse of the altar and the wooden fittings of the martyr’s shrine with pure gold, commemorating the honor of the saint.
And he had craftsmen brought who were masters of their craft.
They worked on the altar to furnish it with gold.
But while they were still working on the wooden fittings, the devil, who hates what is good, struck one of the craftsmen who were working.
He fell down.
The other craftsmen became afraid.
They cried out, “Lord, have mercy!” The emperor and the other people below were shaken by what had happened.
At that very moment, Saint Victor came from heaven, clothed in great glory.
He took hold of the craftsman’s hand before he reached the ground, while he was still three cubits above it.
He lifted him up and went with him to the wooden scaffolding.
He set him on his feet beside the large beam, next to his fellow craftsman.
No harm came to him, and no one saw Saint Victor except the craftsman.
When the emperor and the crowd saw the great miracle that had taken place, they were afraid and cried out, “The God of Saint Victor is one, and there is no other besides him in heaven or on earth!”
When the craftsman recovered from the fear that had seized him, he reported to the emperor and all the people, saying, “I saw a huge Ethiopian,
with his wings spread out,
and his eyes blazing like fire.
He thrust in what he had in his hands and threw me down.
While I was still falling, there appeared a man of light wearing royal clothing, with his face shining like the sun.
He took hold of my hand before I reached the ground.
He went with me and brought me up to this place.”
He made the sign of the cross over me and took away my fear, saying, “Do not be afraid. I am Victor, whose martyr’s shrine you are working on.”
And immediately I stopped seeing him.
When the crowd heard these things, they cried out, “The God of Saint Victor is one!”
And so, through the zeal of the God-loving king and the miracles of Saint Victor,
they furnished the [?] and the altar with pure gold and precious stones of great value.
You have seen, my beloved, how great are the miracles of Saint Victor, whose feast we are celebrating today.
And everyone who appeals to him with all their heart, even if they are suffering from any illness, he grants them healing.
There was also a man in this city who was a patrician in the service of the emperors. He fell ill with an incurable disease.
His whole body swelled up until he was as thick as a pillar.
And it was heartbreaking to see him in this wretched condition.
He was in distress and great, unbearable pain, so that you would often find him sitting down,
with his servants gathered around him. His feet and limbs would burst open and discharge large amounts of foul matter.
And he gave large sums of money to the doctors.
No relief came to him.
Indeed, the emperors of Rome sent chief physicians, because he was an important man in the palace. These men made every effort, but he gained no relief.
While he was in this great suffering, he heard about the miracles and wonders taking place at the sanctuary of Saint Apa Victor.
His servants lifted him up and brought him to the saint’s sanctuary.
They placed him in front of the altar.
And he cried out day and night, saying, “Saint Victor, look upon my misery and my suffering, and grant me healing, for I am suffering terribly.
Or let your mercy reach me, and appeal to God on my behalf, so that he may take me out of this life, for look, you see my distress.” That night,
he dozed off for a short time.
Then Saint Victor took pity on him in his misfortune, because he loves humankind.
He saw him in a vision, clothed in great glory,
wearing a beautiful purple robe and a golden belt,
and sending out rays of light. And he said in the vision, “What illness makes you suffer like this?”
The man said to him, “Look, you see my suffering and my distress, for I have come close to death.”
The saint said to him with a cheerful face, “I am the one who will heal you, so that you may know that I have power to do anything through the grace of God that is with me.”
And he stretched out the staff that was in his hand.
He placed it on the sick man, saying, “Healing has come to you today. But do not continue
to sin, lest something worse than this happen to you.
Do not be hardhearted toward the poor.”
The man answered in alarm, “Who are you, my lord, that you are like this?
I have never seen anyone like you, whether a king or a commander in the palace.”
He answered, “I am Victor, the commander of the King of heaven.”
And when he had said these things to him, the man stopped discharging foul pus, which had soaked his clothing with fluid, and he stopped swelling.
He became as though he had never been sick.
He sprang up and stood on his feet.
He shouted, saying, “The God of Saint Victor is one!”
The crowd gathered in the shrine, when they saw the great wonder,
cried out, “Blessed are we, for we have been deemed worthy of this pearl in our city, healing our illnesses and our afflictions!”
And he gave gifts of gold and silver to the sanctuary of Saint Victor, so that they would distribute them to the poor and the needy.
He went home glorifying God and taking care for the salvation of his soul until the day of his death.
What shall I say about the miracles you have performed, O crown-bearer of Christ?
What tongue of flesh can proclaim your blessedness, O mighty commander?
Truly, even if I spent all my time examining the miracles you have performed, I would not be able to recount even a small part of them.
O confessor and undefeated champion, who can grasp the fullness of your honor and the signs that have occurred in your martyr’s shrine?
For just as no human being can count the honors of this saint and the mighty deeds that continually occur in his sanctuary,
O true crown-bearer of Christ, the young boy whose wisdom surpassed that of the orators!
O you who despised the kingdom of this world so that you might receive the better one, which is the kingdom of heaven!
Great is the glory that God has given you in heaven and on earth.
As I said before, your sweet fragrance has filled all the regions of the world, and your name will be spoken in every region.
From the fortress where you met your end as far as the Cataract, they will honor you throughout the whole world, because you are great among the martyrs.
Above all, God has established lasting signs and wonders in your shrines everywhere.
And there are signs of healing for those who believe in your name, and this same gift continues in your shrines from one end of the inhabited world to the other.
If not, listen, and I will tell you.
Now it happened, they said, when the God-loving emperor Constantine first built the shrine of Saint Apa Victor, where we are gathered today,
that a high-ranking military commander came down with a severe illness.
For six years his internal organs caused him pain, and he could not sleep. He suffered from the disease that physicians call cancer.
He paid approximately more than a hundred pounds of gold to each of the physicians.
He received no benefit at all, but was in danger of dying.
He heard about the miracles and wonders taking place at the shrine of Saint Victor in Antioch.
He got up and went to Antioch.
He spent two days in that shrine without finding healing.
On the night of the third day, he experienced a little rest through the invincible power of God.
Immediately Saint Victor came to him in a vision.
He had the appearance of a mighty general.
His face was sending out rays of light.
He said to him, “If you want to be free of this illness, get up quickly and go to the shrine in Rome.
Then [?] water from the basin at the altar, and you will receive healing.”
“Has the shrine in Rome grown weary, that you have come here? Do you not know that my power is throughout the whole world?”
“This same gift continues in all of them for those who believe without doubting. Do you not know that this same power continues in my shrines,
in Rome and Antioch? Why have you brought this trouble upon yourself?”
“You crossed the open sea and came here.”
“Do you not know that I have the power to heal here?”
“But I will not do this here. You must go to my shrine in Rome and find healing, so that everyone may know my power.”
The man answered, trembling, “My lord, who are you, surrounded by such great glory?”
He answered, “I am Victor the general.”
“I will heal your body and give salvation to your soul.”
Immediately he woke from the vision, trembling greatly.
He said, “Truly, this was Saint Victor, who came to visit me.”
Immediately he repented and said, “Forgive me, my lord Saint Victor, because I neglected to go to your sanctuary, which was newly built in my city, and came here.”
At dawn he woke his servants and the people who had come with him.
He told them about the vision he had seen.
And so he gave great and precious gifts to the shrine in Antioch.
Afterward, he boarded the ship.
He came to the city of Rome.
He entered the shrine of Saint Victor.
He lay down in great distress.
And he was pleading with the God of the holy martyr, saying, “My lord, Saint Victor,
who made me worthy to see his glory in his shrine in Antioch.”
you commanded me to come to this place.
I believe, my lord, that your power fills the whole world, like the sun that shines upon the inhabited earth.
May your mercy reach me, and grant me healing, for I have suffered greatly.”
And after saying these things, he fell asleep in the evening.
Afterward, he had a little water brought to him from the basin of the altar.
He drank it, as Saint Victor had told him, and immediately the God of Saint Victor brought him relief.
He remained oblivious all night, unlike his usual habit.
But at dawn the martyr came to him in great glory.
He said to him with a face
that was cheerful, “Do you recognize me?”
He said to him, “Yes, my lord, I recognize you: you are Saint Victor.
You are the one who appeared to me in your shrine in Antioch.
You sent me to this place.”
The saint said to him, “Did I not tell you before that my power fills every place, and that this same power is present in all my shrines, from one end of the earth to the other,
healing everyone who believes without doubting?
Have you not heard what is written: ‘Everything is possible for the one who believes’?”
The man answered, “I believe, my lord, that your power fills every place. But I heard about the miracles that occur in your shrine in Antioch.
I came seeking healing for my body.”
The saint said to him, “Just as my shrine in Antioch is, so is mine in Rome.
And in all the churches on earth that have been built in my name, from one end of the earth to the other, my power is at work within them among those who believe, until the end of this age.”
I heal hidden illnesses and visible ones through the grace that God gave me and all the saints.
Now, look: I have granted you healing. So now pay attention to the salvation of your soul, so that something worse than this does not happen to you.
When Saint Apa Victor had said these things to the man, he hid himself from him.
He woke up at dawn.
He fell ill and suffered a rupture in his inner part, namely the [?].
He discharged a large amount of pus from his mouth.
He immediately recovered completely from his illness.
And he spread the news throughout the whole city of what Saint Victor had said to him.
And from that day onward, anyone sick with a disease, with any disease, who goes to the saint's shrine is granted healing by him.
The man gave great gifts to the sanctuary of Saint Victor.
He went home glorifying God, and he kept asking Saint Victor to help him in all his troubles, fasting and praying until the day of his death.
You have seen, my beloved, how powerful the miracles of this saint are, whose feast we celebrate today.
And these powers are at work in all his martyr shrines for those who believe.
Let us too believe with all our hearts in the powers and miracles of this saint, so that he will intercede for us before God.
For anyone who disbelieves in the powers of the saints will not only receive no benefit, but it will bring condemnation upon him. Now, so that we do not prolong the account,
let us return and tell you about this other great miracle that happened at the shrine of Saint Apa Victor, to the glory of God and his saint.
There was a man in this city whose name was Anastasius.
He was very wealthy and held in honor among his family.
After he had grown old and reached seventy years of age,
he contracted the disease that physicians call elephantiasis.
And he became [?] all over and leprous, white as snow, so that he was often ashamed before the people who saw him, because his body had become spotted like a leopard.
He was deeply distressed about this, because he was ashamed to go to the palace or to appear in the marketplace because of what had happened to him.
After this, God put it into his heart to go to the martyr’s shrine of the holy Father Victor and plead with him, so that he would surely heal him of his illness.
Since he saw some people suffering from various illnesses,
and whenever they went to his martyr shrine, they received healing and went home glorifying [?] God,
he therefore got up in faith.
He went to the shrine of Saint Apa Victor with his servants and substantial offerings.
He spent two days in the holy place, pleading with Saint Victor to have mercy on him and heal him of his leprosy.
And he said, “Saint Victor, I believe with all my heart that you have the power to heal me of this leprosy.”
Help me, because I am ashamed to have anyone see me because of what has happened to me.
When he had spent two days in the shrine, there was a man whose eyes were inflamed. Because of the severity of his suffering, white patches had developed in his eyes.
He could no longer see with his own eyes.
He had spent everything he owned on doctors.
But he had received no cure.
Finally, when he heard about the miracles of Saint Victor, he had people take him to his shrine, while he was suffering greatly.
They laid him on a bed beside the man with leprosy.
And he pleaded with the God of Saint Victor, saying, “My lord, the commander, have mercy on me and grant light to my eyes.”
We cannot remain silent about the miracle that happened at that time.
That night, God heard everyone who sincerely called upon him, and he was pleased to heal the two men together,
through the intercessions of Saint Victor, who performs these wonders and mighty deeds.
That night, after the man with leprosy had eaten with his servants and they had gone to sleep and become oblivious, Saint Victor took pity on the suffering of the man with leprosy and the blind man.
He chose to reveal his miracles.
He came to the man with leprosy at night, clothed in great glory, with his face shining very brightly.
He said to him, “Do you recognize who I am?”
He answered, “No, my lord.”
The saint said to him, “I am Victor, the one you plead with every day.”
“I am the father of the shrine.”
“Now, if you want to be cleansed of leprosy, when you get up in the morning, take the hand of this blind man sleeping beside you,
and lead him down to the pool at the entrance to the shrine.”
“Immerse yourselves in it three times, in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.”
“And you will see my power: your leprosy will leave you, and the blind man will see.”
Only do not neglect what he told you, and you will recover.
When Saint Victor had said these things to the leper, he left him.
Immediately he awoke from the vision, trembling with fear.
And he smelled a strong, pleasant fragrance around his sleeping place, like fine incense.
He said to himself, “Truly, it was Saint Victor who came to me to grant me healing.”
And he rejoiced greatly and blessed God. But he kept the matter in his heart, saying, “I will not tell anyone about the vision.”
He was waiting to see how the matter would turn out.
When daylight came, the man with leprosy said to the blind man, “Will you get up so that we can go down to the cistern and bathe?”
“And I believe in God and his holy martyr, that he will grant us healing.”
The blind man said to the man with leprosy, “Do as you wish.”
No, look, you see my suffering and my distress.
But I am afraid to bathe, because the doctors have instructed me not to pour water over my head.
The leper said to the blind man, “Get up and let us bathe. God is able to remember us and grant us healing, because we have suffered.”
The blind man agreed to what he said, and the leper took his hand in the midst of the entire crowd.
They went down to the cistern from which the basins of the place are filled.
They immersed themselves three times, saying, “In the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the holy martyr, Saint Victor.”
Immediately the leper was healed, and his flesh became like that of a little child.
As for the blind man, the white films in his eyes peeled away.
They fell down into the pool, and his sight was fully restored.
They cried out, saying, “The God of Saint Victor is one, and he heals everyone through his holy power!”
When the crowd gathered at the martyr’s shrine heard them, they hurried out toward them, looking at the great miracle that had taken place.
They cried out, “Great are the mighty works of God and Saint Victor!
Great is the favor God has shown us!
We have been found worthy of your martyr’s shrine in our city!” Then, when they were told what had happened to them,
the leper reported everything to them, including how Saint Victor had spoken with him in the vision.
News of this miracle spread everywhere, and I saw it with my own eyes,
I, the least of all, who am speaking to you in this tribute.
Now the leper and the blind man, who had received healing through Saint Victor,
remained serving at his shrine until the day of his death, and they received their food for the salvation of their souls.
And in the pool where they had bathed, a great power of God has remained active to this very day,
so that anyone who is sick, whether paralyzed or possessed by a demon—in short, suffering from any illness—
receives healing as soon as they bathe in that pool, and they go home glorifying the God of Saint Victor.
What shall I say, and what shall I leave out, among your achievements?
Who among all the philosophers of the world will be able to praise you as you deserve,
O you who offered your body as a living, holy, acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God?
You endured great sufferings for the name of Christ, O noble Apa Victor.
Great is the glory God has given you in heaven and on earth.
Truly, the written word has been fulfilled: “The sufferings of the present time are not worthy of the glory that will be revealed to us.”
Great is the honor God has given you, O holy commander, so that everyone who calls upon God in your name,
whatever distress they may be in, is quickly reached by God’s help, even to this very moment.
He saves everyone who begs him with all their heart from every danger. If you do not believe it, listen, and I will tell you.
Now it happened that the barbarians called Saban rose up against the territory of the Roman Empire, as numerous as the sand of the sea,
so that they took the first region of the Roman Empire and prepared many ships to cross over and come against us in the Roman Empire.
Now all the people, the senate, the entire citizen body of Rome, and all the nearby surrounding districts,
They were [?], holding the general service at the shrine of Saint Victor, where we are now gathered.
The God-loving king was there with his army of soldiers, because it was the feast of Saint Victor. My father Innocent was also there with all the clergy.
When they began the service with great awe, letters were sent to the emperor
through a courier named Frumentius, which the prefects of First Romania had sent to him.
They said, “Quickly prepare your army, reach us without delay, and help us, for the barbarians have captured First Armenia.”
The emperor was immediately troubled, as any human would be, but all his hope rested on the Lord.
When he read the letter, he immediately wrote to the governors, “Do not be afraid. I am coming tomorrow morning with the entire Roman population.”
When the courier had received the letter and departed,
the emperor and all the people gathered at the sanctuary of Saint Victor, together with the archbishop and all the clergy.
They laid them on the altar, saying, “Saint Victor, the general,
appeal to God on our behalf, so that he may fortify our country and the godless barbarians may not overpower it.”
In this way they held a great general worship service, prolonging it until the tenth hour of the day.
The miracle that happened at that time is beyond description.
When they had finished, and the archbishop was about to give the people the greeting of peace before they departed for their homes,
another senior courier arrived, whom the governors had sent to the emperor with another letter, in great joy. It was written as follows: “Peace to you, God-loving emperor!
Be victorious and prevail, for God fights on your behalf.
Look, the godless barbarians who rose against your empire—
God has struck them down with their own swords.
Each one rose against the person beside him, beginning at the second hour today.
They killed one another. Not one of them survived; they all died.
We have sent all their equipment and their horses to Your Majesty.
Therefore, do not trouble yourself or disturb the military command, for God is the one who fights for us and for you.
Who can oppose us?”
When the emperor received this letter, he read it to the people before they departed.
They rejoiced exceedingly, with great joy, and immediately understood that Saint Victor, the commander, was the one who had struck down the barbarians,
since it was at the second hour of the day that they had begged him.
They all cried out in a loud voice, giving glory to God and to Saint Victor. And the barbarians did not continue to invade Roman territory, down to this very day.
You have seen, my beloved, how great is the power of the holy commander whose feast we celebrate today.
Let us turn away from every evil deed, every act of violence, every kind of disorder, and every deception that we practice, so that we may all become his children together.
Truly, you have made us glad today, Saint Victor the general, more than those who celebrate in places where wine is drunk,
for you have set before us the table of your holy feast, filled with every good thing.
Let us, for our part, recognize these things and taste them, so that we may rejoice.
Let us remember the sufferings that our Lord endured for us, together with his servants, the martyrs,
and let us offer fruit to God as he deserves, each according to their ability: one through purity, another through prayer and fasting,
one through endurance, another through cheerfulness, another through love and hospitality.
In short, let none of us remain without bearing fruit, so that we may become God's field and sow within ourselves the fruits of righteousness.
Listen to the wise apostle Paul,
who says, "I urge you, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living, holy sacrifice, pleasing to God."
How will we present our bodies, Saint Victor, unless we keep our body and our heart free from every deception and every kind of sexual immorality?
For it is written, "Without purity, no one will see God."
And let us guard our mouth so that we do not slander, lie, or say any obscene word.
Train your hands, too, for prayer, and keep them from theft and violence.
Let your feet, too, run to the threshold of God's house.
Guard your eyes so that you do not lust or stumble because of women.
When you observe all these things, you will truly be able to offer your body confidently as a sacrifice to the Lord,
like Saint Victor, who renounced the world and everything in it because of his love for God.
Listen to Peter, the foremost apostle,
who says, "I urge you, my brothers, as strangers and foreigners, to keep away from fleshly desires, which fight against your souls."
So then, my beloved, we are foreigners on the earth.
So then, a person walks about as an image, gathering things without knowing for whom he gathers them.
If we are strangers and foreigners on earth, then we ought to keep thinking about our eternal home, which is the kingdom of God.
We will enter it with ease if we keep the commandments entrusted to us.
We were born [?] to inherit the earth, but for the earth to inherit [?].
For the earth is the home of every human being.
Since we entered this world weeping, we will also leave weeping. We came sighing, and we will also leave sighing.
For from the very first hour when a person is born into the world, he weeps.
And again, when he leaves the body, he weeps. We were born into suffering, and we will go again into suffering.
For there is nothing lasting in human life except misery and sorrow.
Have you not heard what is written?
"Do not let your heart become weighed down with overeating, drunkenness, and the worries of life, so that that day comes upon you like a trap."
For it is coming upon everyone who lives on the face of the whole earth, whether king or ruler, rich or poor. Not a single person will escape that terrifying ordeal.
Do you not listen to what is written: “Money will not benefit us on the day of wrath”?
Righteousness saves a person from death.
Do not put your confidence in money or in the pride of wealth.
Do not bolster your soul with rule and authority.
Furthermore, gold or silver—all these are chains.
For money will not remain here, but our sins will go ahead of us and stand before God's judgment seat.
Have you yourself not heard what the Lord said: “Keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour”?
Let us therefore keep watch day and night, because we are not masters of our bodies for even a single hour.
And we do not know when we will be sought out.
Do not let us base our security on the illusions of wealth. You do not know when you will be summoned.
Have you not heard what is written: “No person can pay a ransom; no brother can redeem a brother”?
He will not give God his ransom or the price for redeeming his soul.
He makes this known: no righteous father can redeem a sinful son, nor can a rich brother redeem a poor brother,
nor can a righteous son redeem a sinful father. Rather, each will receive according to what they have done.
Now then, my beloved, send your wealth ahead of you through acts of mercy toward the poor, so that you may find unending enjoyment.
Do not put your trust in the wealth of this world.
Do not make gold and silver your foundation.
Have you not heard Solomon
saying: “I hated all my wealth, for which I labored under the sun, because I must leave it to the person who comes after me”?
That is, scarcely would a foolish person say within his soul: “I am gathering things for my children, so that they will find their livelihood after my death.”
How do you know, you fool, that your son will live and inherit from you, or that he will acquire a great fortune and give it away?
Will God not care for your children without you?
Will the God who fed you not also feed your children?
On the day you were born, was even a single obol born along with you?
Now then, God has graciously given you this great wealth so that you may find rest here and in the world beyond, but Satan has closed your heart.
He has not allowed you to be merciful toward the poor. Because of this, you will receive great, unending punishments for your lack of faith.
For we have seen many rich people accumulating wealth through great toil and trading, building large houses for themselves,
along with properties, extensive estates, gardens, fields, and many livestock,
as well as abundant household goods and great wealth, saying, “We are storing these things up for our children.”
And while they were still thinking about these things, their children were snatched from them in their childhood.
Strangers seized the fruits of their labor, and they themselves
went naked to God's judgment seat, with no good deeds before them and no gift in their hands.
They cursed the day on which they were born into the world.
Do not say in your stubbornness, “When I leave the body,
I will write my will so that my children and relatives give charity for my soul.”
O senseless and utterly foolish person! Do you not know that when you leave the body, you will not own a single obol, nor will anyone remember you again?
You no longer have the money you stored up.
You no longer have a full storehouse.
You no longer have vineyards.
You no longer have the houses you built; instead, you have become a stranger to them.
They have ceased to be yours.
They have become the property of others.
If they wish, they give on your behalf; if they do not wish, they do not give on your behalf.
Have you not heard the holy Job
saying, “I came naked from my mother's womb, and I will go away naked again”?
The apostle also cries out, saying, “We brought nothing with us into this world, and we will take nothing when we leave.”
David also says, “Their spirit leaves them, and they return to their earth.”
O miserable person, you are like this! What are these anxieties and these cares?
For you know the place of your birth, but you do not know the place of your death.
You know how many years you have lived until now, but you do not know how many more you will live.
You know how your parents, who brought you into the world, died.
Now then, O person, accept my advice, and let my counsel be pleasing to you: redeem your sins through acts of charity,
and your lawless deeds through acts of compassion toward the poor, so that you may enjoy everlasting wealth.
Send gifts ahead of you before you leave the body, so that you may meet Christ with joy.
For a person who is going to meet a king of this world and find favor with him
sends gifts ahead of himself so that the king will welcome him.
How much more should we send acts of charity ahead of us to the King of all, whom fear and trembling surround!
Solomon says, “Keep all your provisions at hand.”
Give to the poor according to your ability.
Do not say, “I have nothing to give.”
Remember the poor widow who put two small coins into the treasury.
And Christ honored her because she gave all that she lacked.
He also said, “Whoever gives one of these little ones even a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple—truly I tell you, he will not lose his reward.”
So do not neglect your salvation, O human being, for the sake of the material things of this life. They will not leave us here forever.
Rather, a day will come when we leave it and become as though we had never entered it.
Remember the time when the sickness of death will come upon you, and you will immediately throw yourself onto your bed and say, “I am sick today.”
Suddenly, illness weighs down upon you, and a great fever seizes your wretched flesh, together with severe distress and suffering.
Your bodily condition is thrown into disorder, your tongue grows small in your throat, and your speech dwindles in your mouth.
Your throat stiffens, and no food enters it. The light of your eyes fades little by little, and saliva gathers around your throat.
Great bitterness fills your heart, and the functioning of your eyes ceases. They roll and grow dim, for the light has gradually left them.
You ask those who are visiting you, “What time is it?” because your awareness has ceased within you.
Darkness and mist have covered your eyes.
Your face has changed and become pale.
The hair has come loose.
The sinews of your hands and feet have stiffened.
Your heart and your soul have weakened little by little.
You signal with your eyes, looking out for the powers with changing faces that have come for you, hurrying to take you to the one who created you.
And when you see them, you open your mouth and give your spirit into the hands of the one who has come for you.
Oh, this great wonder and this great ordeal, more distressing than every ordeal on earth!
Oh, the anguish that surpasses every anguish—the fear of death!
Then they take the soul and bring it before the fearful judgment seat of God, so that it may receive according to what it has done, whether good or evil.
O wise apostle Paul, your words are very sweet!
For every person whom God has created, from Adam, the first human being, down to the one who will be born today—when they leave the body,
Their souls are taken and brought before the judgment seat of God, from the one a month old to the one a year old.
They bow before the true Judge, and he pronounces sentence upon them before they are taken to the places they deserve.
And again, on the day of the resurrection, their bodies will rise imperishable.
And everyone’s soul will return to their bodies once more, and they will receive according to what they have done, whether good or evil.
And we will be called to account for everything we have done in this place of exile, down to a little joking remark.
They will also be questioned about the thoughts of the heart, just as our teacher and maker, Christ, said:
“Do not let any idle words come out of your mouths, for you will give an account of them on the day of judgment.”
Blessed are those who will rise to a resurrection of life, for they will reign with Christ.
Woe to those who will be condemned to the second death because of their evil deeds!
But when the true judge stands at the judgment seat, whoever has passed away has passed away.
But the straw will be burned in a fire that cannot be extinguished.
But the wheat will be gathered into the storehouse, which is the kingdom of heaven.
Now, then, let us turn back and repent of our sins before we are sought out.
Remember that it is a terrifying thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
Tell me, then, what are all these schemes and all these hardships?
Is our everlasting home not three cubits of earth?
For whom are you gathering things?
For whom are you collecting interest?
For whom are you breaking the law?
Tell me, who will send these things down to you in the underworld?
Remember that you are not your own master for even a single day, but you [?] on this earth like a day laborer.
And whether you eat or drink, whether you fast, whether you are hungry or thirsty, the sun sets every day, and your lifetime is shortened every day.
And when the number of your days is complete, you will not be allowed even one more hour.
A human being is absolutely nothing.
A human being today; tomorrow, earth and ashes.
The one who eats and drinks today will have his mouth shut tomorrow.
The one who is eating right now and bathing in oils, anointing himself with choice perfumes today, will himself be rolled into the tombs tomorrow.
Dust became perfume for him.
The one who slept among purple fabrics, covered with linen garments, was thrown out the next day among the tombs and the wild animals.
They turned their backs on him.
They left him in poverty.
O poor man, food and drink could not rescue you today. Why did the riches of your wealth not save you and provide you with a little care?
Why did the displays of your wealth not save you in these great hardships?
Have you not heard about that foolish rich man, who was just like you, who said to his soul:
“You have many good things stored up for many years. Rest, eat, drink, and enjoy yourself”—thinking that he would spend a long time on earth.
Immediately God's sentence overtook him: “Fool, they will take your soul tonight. Whose will the things you have prepared be?”
This is how it is with everyone who stores things up but is not rich in God.
Why, then, fool, could your full storehouses not rescue you today?
Why could your garments of pure silk and linen not save you today?
Why could the riches you gathered up not prevent God's sentence from overtaking you: “They will take your soul tonight”?
Have you not heard David say, “They will leave their wealth to others, and their tombs are their homes forever”?
Wise Solomon says, “Have all your preparations ready, for there is neither knowledge nor thought in Hades, the place where you are going.” This means:
When you leave this world, you will not be able to put anything right. Instead, the things you took with you when you left are the things by which and for which you will be judged.
Tell me, then, fool, what are all these deceptions and these sins? You pile sin upon sin, lawlessness upon lawlessness, deceit upon deceit, and strife upon strife.
Have you not remembered what is written: “Judgment is without mercy for the one who has shown no mercy”?
Remember that a human being is like a shadow, and that his days pass swiftly.
A person's entire lifetime is like the steam from a pot: it appears for a little while and afterward disappears—especially the person who commits sin.
There is no benefit in the life of evildoers, nor will such a person find any in the place where he is going. Instead, he will go from suffering to suffering.
Even if he is a rich sinner, there is no rest in his life.
Have you not heard Solomon say, “He came in futility, and he will go away again in futility. He came in sorrow, and he will go away again in sorrow”?
As it is written, “There is no joy for the ungodly,” says the Lord, and again, “The hope of the ungodly will perish.”
And again: “The ungodly person is like chaff that the wind blows away from the face of the earth.”
Tell me, then, O sinner, what joy has come to you throughout your whole life?
If you say, “I spent my whole life rich and enjoying myself thoroughly,” I will say to you briefly:
“What joy did you find throughout all your time, while you were living in sin,
Even if you are rich in gold and silver, what benefit have you gained from being born on earth?
This man, indeed, is eating and drinking today.
The next day he too was carried away amid his wealth. They shut his mouth so that he would not eat from that moment on.
Tell me, you sinful man, what rest do you have, since you spend all your time distracted, collecting interest and trading?
You worry day and night like someone who lacks bread.
There is no comfort around you; instead, your whole life is sorrow.
building houses, estates, and granaries, and planting vineyards and gardens,
and watering places, working as a merchant and sailing on the sea, always like those in the agony of death?”
You oppress the poor.
You throw stones at strangers.
You seize the houses of widows, and you are distracted day and night.
Yet what you eat is bread, just like everyone else.
And while you are doing these things, the appointed span of your life comes to an end. They wrap you up like a [?] and carry you away.
The wealth you have gathered will remain here, and the sins you have committed will go before you to God's judgment seat.
The houses you built are images that expose your foolishness; others will live in them.
But your soul will be carried away into the outer darkness because of your lawless deeds.
Others will harvest the vineyards you planted, while you long for a drop from them to moisten your tongue in Hades, like your brother Nineveh.
Tell me now, you merciless and sinful person: what have you gained by being born into the world,
either in your life or in your death, except the punishments you have piled up for yourself because of your sins?
During your life you are distracted day and night,
toiling to increase your wealth. Then, at your death, you have gone to endless punishments in repayment for your lawless deeds.
If, on the other hand, the sinner is poor, you will find him working night and day because of the deprivation of his poverty.
His children are hungry and naked, and his wife is hungry and worn down by suffering. They curse one another.
There is no peace among them.
They are distracted day and night, living in distress with their children.
He often longs for death because of the suffering he is in.
Seeing his poverty, his wife’s suffering, and his children’s distress, he sins all the more,
with thefts and false oaths, as it is written: “Poverty humbles a person.”
And not only does it humble him, but it makes him practice deceit and do things that God hates, because he wants to bring something home for his wife and children.
And so he never stops being distracted by these worries throughout his entire life.
He adds sin to sin, spending his life until the allotted time of his life is complete and he is suddenly taken away.
He is loaded down with the burden of his sins and departs in poverty, into endless poverty and great suffering.
Tell me now: what benefit does this person gain from being born into the world, other than suffering, misery, and anguish?
This is the one about whom it was written: “He came in futility, and he will go in futility, and his name will be covered in darkness.” Yet whether rich or poor,
woe to them for having been born into the world, because their coming into the world has become a loss to them.
What comfort will there be for the person who dies in his sins, other than suffering and anguish in this place and the other place?
Have you not heard what is written in Isaiah the prophet: “The sinner will reach a hundred years and be cursed”?
But tell me when you ever rejoiced, you sinful person.
Did you rejoice while you were in your mother’s womb?
How could you rejoice, shut up in darkness and stench, knowing neither day nor night?
Did you rejoice when you came out of your mother’s womb?
How could you rejoice?
For from the moment you were born, you were weeping and crying out.
For if you were comfortable, you would not weep. Weeping belongs to suffering.
Did you rejoice while you were being nursed at your mother’s breasts?
How could you rejoice?
You were crying all the time, with no understanding in you.
Did you rejoice when you were little?
How could you rejoice?
Your face was always bent down toward the ground as you crawled on your hands and feet.
Your mouth was dripping saliva, and if an animal trampled on you and killed you, you would not understand.
Did you rejoice when your knees grew strong and you began to walk?
How could you rejoice?
Your parents were disciplining you, sending you to a teacher so that you would learn a trade and make your living from it.
Did you rejoice when you grew up and reached adulthood?
How will you rejoice?
When the passions of childhood within you fight against you and do not let you rest for even a single hour.
Did you rejoice when you took a wife?
No, you did not rejoice. Instead, you had even more worries piled upon you.
Did you rejoice when you had children?
How will you rejoice?
When you bear worry upon worry, day and night.
For the man who has married and fathered children does not have a single hour of rest.
Instead, worries weigh on him all his life. Especially if he is poor, his troubles multiply upon him.
Did you rejoice when you grew old?
How will you rejoice?
When your bones have grown weak, the light of your eyes has gone out, the teeth have fallen out and stopped grinding food, and the mind has stopped perceiving
and understanding a word of wisdom, the body’s sinews have loosened and can no longer manage to rise easily.
The mouth closed and stopped speaking well. The voice grew weak. The ears stopped hearing.
All these things have come upon you in your old age, especially another great sorrow: you have drawn near to the grave, and you do not know how long people will seek you.
Did you rejoice when your allotted time came to an end, because you were going to stand before God?
How will you rejoice at that moment?
When you lie upon the bed of your distress.
When a great fever surrounds you and a severe illness weighs upon you, and you sigh over your sins because you have no good deeds before you.
When you grieve for your little children who will become orphans.
When you are troubled by the distress that is upon you.
When you look at the powers with shifting faces that have come for you.
When you sigh over the end of your life because it has come suddenly.
Did you rejoice, O man, as you stood before the judgment seat of God?
How will you rejoice when you are weighed down by the burden of your sins?
You have no good deeds before you.
When the angels of punishment seize your soul, and their eyes shoot out flames of fire.
They snarl at you and gnash their teeth at you.
Your sins follow you, serving as your accusers.
Where will you turn your face, O poor man? Or where will you look while you are being laid to rest, when there is neither right nor left?
Look at the poor whom you oppressed.
Look at the needy and the strangers whom you mocked.
You consumed what belonged to them.
Look at the false oaths.
Look at the slanders.
Look at the hatred.
Look at the jealousies.
Look at the quarrels.
Look at the defilements.
Look at the impurities.
Look at the acts of sexual immorality.
Look at the murders and all the other evil deeds you committed.
Then, at that moment, the judge cries out, “Throw him into the outer darkness. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth there.”
This is the end of every sinner who did not repent of their sins before dying.
Look, I have made the matter clear to you: there is no profit in a person's life, in having been born into this world.
If you want to be saved and inherit life, hurry and redeem your sins through acts of mercy
and compassion toward the poor, so that you may enjoy yourself in the place where there is joy and gladness.
And even if you have committed every sin, turn back and repent. God will forgive you.
For he is merciful and loves humanity. He relents over the evils of those who turn back to him.
He says, “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he turn away from his evil way, repent, and live.”
And again: “If the lawless person turns away from his wicked deeds and practices righteousness…”
I will not remember the lawless deeds he committed. Rather, he will live by the righteousness he practiced.
He says, “Return to me, children who have strayed, and I will heal your brokenness.”
He says with his mouth, which is full of life, “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”
And again, “Come to me, all who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.”
Have you seen God's love for humanity toward us, O human being?
So then, do not keep adding day after day, month after month, year after year, until the allotted span of your life runs out,
and you depart loaded with the punishment for your sins and curse the day you were born.
I have said all these things to you, my beloved, because of the written saying: “A person is born to suffering.”

So every year he would give large quantities of wine to the shrine, for celebrating the liturgy and distributing to the sick and those in need, for the salvation of his soul.

Now God, who is good, through the intercessions of Saint Victor,
